summary.text: For general $k$, any admissible $m<2^{2^k+1}$ has $\varphi(m)=2^{2^k}$; the bound $2\varphi(m)\le m$ for even $m$ makes $m$ odd, after which $m$ is squarefree and every prime divisor is a Fermat number $F_i$ with $i\le k$.  If $F_k\nmid m$, the Fermat product identity gives $m\le\prod_{i<k}F_i=2^{2^k}-1<\varphi(m)$, so necessarily $m=F_k$ and $F_k$ is prime; since $2^{2^k+1}$ is always admissible, this yields the required dichotomy at $k=33$.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 a(n)=\min\{m\in\mathbb N:m>0\text{ and }2^n\mid \varphi(m)\},
\]
where \(\varphi\) is Euler's totient function. We prove the stronger assertion that for every nonnegative integer \(k\),
\[
 a(2^k)=
 \begin{cases}
 F_k,&\text{if }F_k\text{ is prime},\\[2mm]
 2^{2^k+1},&\text{if }F_k\text{ is not prime},
 \end{cases}
 \tag{1}
\]
where
\[
 F_k=2^{2^k}+1
\]
is the \(k\)-th Fermat number. Taking \(k=33\) gives the claimed result.

We begin with several elementary facts about the totient function that will be used in the proof. For every positive integer \(m\),
\[
 1\leq \varphi(m)\leq m.
 \tag{2}
\]
If \(p\) is prime and \(e\geq 1\), then
\[
 \varphi(p^e)=p^{e-1}(p-1).
 \tag{3}
\]
Also, if \(d\mid m\), then
\[
 \varphi(d)\mid \varphi(m).
 \tag{4}
\]
For completeness, (4) follows directly from prime factorizations. Write the exponent of a prime \(p\) in \(d\) and \(m\) as \(f_p\) and \(e_p\), respectively. Since \(d\mid m\), one has \(f_p\leq e_p\). If \(f_p>0\), then the local factor \(p^{f_p-1}(p-1)\) in \(\varphi(d)\) divides the local factor \(p^{e_p-1}(p-1)\) in \(\varphi(m)\); primes absent from \(d\) contribute the factor 1. Multiplying these divisibilities over the distinct primes gives (4).

We will also need the following sharper estimate when \(m\) is even:
\[
 2\varphi(m)\leq m.
 \tag{5}
\]
One way to prove it is by induction on the even positive integer \(m\). Write \(m=2r\). If \(r\) is odd, then \(\varphi(2r)=\varphi(r)\), and hence by (2)
\[
 2\varphi(m)=2\varphi(r)\leq 2r=m.
\]
If \(r\) is even, then \(\varphi(2r)=2\varphi(r)\). Applying the induction hypothesis to the smaller even integer \(r\) gives \(2\varphi(r)\leq r\), and consequently
\[
 2\varphi(m)=4\varphi(r)\leq 2r=m.
\]
This proves (5).

Fix now a nonnegative integer \(k\), and abbreviate
\[
 T=2^{2^k},\qquad F_k=T+1,
 \qquad B=2T=2^{2^k+1}.
 \tag{6}
\]
Thus an integer is admissible for \(a(2^k)\) precisely when it is positive and \(T\mid\varphi(m)\). Notice first that \(B\) is always admissible. Indeed, \(B=2^{2^k+1}\), so by the prime-power formula (3),
\[
 \varphi(B)=\varphi\bigl(2^{2^k+1}\bigr)=2^{2^k}=T.
 \tag{7}
\]
In particular, the set defining \(a(2^k)\) is nonempty.

The heart of the proof is the following classification.

**Claim.** If \(m>0\), \(T\mid\varphi(m)\), and \(m<B\), then
\[
 m=F_k
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 F_k\text{ is prime}.
 \tag{8}
\]

We prove the claim in several steps.

First, since \(T\mid\varphi(m)\) and \(\varphi(m)>0\), we have \(T\leq\varphi(m)\). On the other hand, by (2) and the assumption \(m<B=2T\),
\[
 \varphi(m)\leq m<2T.
\]
The only positive multiple of \(T\) that is strictly less than \(2T\) is \(T\) itself. Therefore
\[
 \varphi(m)=T.
 \tag{9}
\]

Second, \(m\) must be odd. If it were even, (5) and (9) would give
\[
 2T=2\varphi(m)\leq m,
\]
contradicting \(m<2T\).

Third, \(m\) is squarefree. Suppose to the contrary that \(p^2\mid m\) for some prime \(p\). By (4),
\[
 \varphi(p^2)\mid\varphi(m).
\]
Using (3) and (9), this says
\[
 p(p-1)\mid T=2^{2^k}.
\]
In particular, \(p\mid 2^{2^k}\). Since \(p\) is prime, this forces \(p=2\). But then \(2\mid m\), contradicting the fact that \(m\) is odd. Thus no prime square divides \(m\), proving that \(m\) is squarefree.

Fourth, we classify all prime divisors of \(m\). Let \(p\mid m\) be prime. By (4),
\[
 \varphi(p)=p-1\mid\varphi(m)=2^{2^k}.
\]
Every divisor of a power of 2 is a power of 2, so
\[
 p-1=2^j
 \quad\text{for some }0\leq j\leq 2^k.
 \tag{10}
\]
Because \(m\) is odd, \(p\neq 2\), and hence \(j\neq0\).

We use the standard elementary observation that if \(2^j+1\) is prime and \(j>0\), then \(j\) itself is a power of 2. To see this, write
\[
 j=2^i q
\]
with \(q\) odd. If \(q>1\), set \(x=2^{2^i}\). Then
\[
 2^j+1=x^q+1.
\]
Since \(q\) is odd,
\[
 x^q+1=(x+1)(x^{q-1}-x^{q-2}+\cdots-x+1),
\]
and when \(q>1\) this is a nontrivial factorization. Thus \(2^j+1\) could not be prime. Consequently \(q=1\), so \(j=2^i\).

Applying this to \(p=2^j+1\), we obtain
\[
 p=2^{2^i}+1=F_i
\]
for some \(i\). The bound \(j\leq2^k\) in (10) becomes \(2^i\leq2^k\), and hence \(i\leq k\). We have therefore shown:
\[
 \text{every prime divisor of }m\text{ is one of }F_0,F_1,\ldots,F_k.
 \tag{11}
\]
Only those Fermat numbers that happen to be prime can of course occur as prime divisors, but (11) is all that is needed.

We next prove that \(F_k\mid m\). Suppose instead that \(F_k\nmid m\). Since every prime divisor of \(m\) is among \(F_0,\ldots,F_k\), this supposition excludes \(F_k\) itself from the prime divisors of \(m\). Since \(m\) is squarefree, \(m\) is then a product of a subset of \(F_0,\ldots,F_{k-1}\). Hence
\[
 m\mid\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}F_i.
 \tag{12}
\]
The Fermat numbers satisfy the identity
\[
 \prod_{i=0}^{k-1}F_i=F_k-2=2^{2^k}-1=T-1.
 \tag{13}
\]
This identity also includes \(k=0\), when the product is empty and equals 1. It follows by induction: if the product through \(F_{k-1}\) is \(2^{2^k}-1\), then multiplying by
\(F_k=2^{2^k}+1\) gives
\[
 (2^{2^k}-1)(2^{2^k}+1)=2^{2^{k+1}}-1,
\]
which is the next case.

From (12) and (13), positivity gives \(m\leq T-1\). But (9) and (2) give
\[
 T=\varphi(m)\leq m,
\]
a contradiction. Therefore
\[
 F_k\mid m.
 \tag{14}
\]

Since \(F_k=T+1\) and \(m<2T<2(T+1)=2F_k\), the only positive multiple of \(F_k\) that \(m\) can be is \(F_k\) itself. Thus
\[
 m=F_k.
 \tag{15}
\]
Finally, (9), (15), and \(F_k=T+1\) yield
\[
 \varphi(F_k)=T=F_k-1.
 \tag{16}
\]
For every integer \(n>1\), equality \(\varphi(n)=n-1\) holds if and only if \(n\) is prime: if \(n\) is prime, all of \(1,\ldots,n-1\) are coprime to it; conversely, if \(n\) is composite, a proper divisor between 1 and \(n\) is not coprime to \(n\), so fewer than \(n-1\) residues are counted. Since \(F_k>2\), (16) proves that \(F_k\) is prime. This completes the proof of the claim.

It remains to identify the minimum, and here there are two cases.

**Case 1: \(F_k\) is prime.** Then
\[
 \varphi(F_k)=F_k-1=T,
\]
so \(F_k\) is admissible. We show no admissible positive integer is smaller. Let \(m\) be any admissible integer. If \(m<B\), the claim says \(m=F_k\). If \(m\geq B\), then
\[
 m\geq B=2T\geq T+1=F_k,
\]
where the middle inequality follows from \(T\geq1\). Thus every admissible \(m\) is at least \(F_k\), and \(F_k\) itself is admissible. Therefore
\[
 a(2^k)=F_k.
 \tag{17}
\]

**Case 2: \(F_k\) is not prime.** Equation (7) shows that \(B=2^{2^k+1}\) is admissible. If there were an admissible \(m<B\), the claim would imply that \(F_k\) is prime, contrary to the assumption. Hence every admissible integer is at least \(B\), and so
\[
 a(2^k)=B=2^{2^k+1}.
 \tag{18}
\]

Equations (17) and (18) prove (1) for every \(k\). In particular, set \(k=33\), put
\[
 N=2^{33},\qquad F_{33}=2^{2^{33}}+1.
\]
Then
\[
 a(2^{33})=
 \begin{cases}
 F_{33},&\text{if }F_{33}\text{ is prime},\\[2mm]
 2^{2^{33}+1},&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
This is exactly the stated conjecture.
